newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-FREDIA "THE CHEETAH" COMING TO A LIVING ROOM NEAR YOU.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-FREDIA "THE CHEETAH" COMING TO A LIVING ROOM NEAR YOU.

text.p: First there was "Lips of Rouge, Fists of Fury." Now it's "Leather and Lace", coming to a television screen in your living room.
Quick! Cover the children's eyes! Call in the porn police! Rally the religious right!
Fredia "The Cheetah", "Pulverizing" Paula, Christina "Crunch" and "Baby Doll" want to seduce us into spending a little time with them -- for a price, of course.
Do we need any more proof that Sodom and Gomorrah are around the corner from Main Street?
Nah, it's just boxing. Women's version.
Of course, in the eyes of some people that proves the point: when women put on boxing gloves all hope is lost for civilisation.
Regardless, promoters say there is a burgeoning market these days for power-punching women.

And Rick Kulis, president of Event Entertainment, is betting that his "Leather and Lace" all-women, eight-bout card this Saturday night in Biloxi, Mississippi -- its first all-women fight card since "Lips of Rouge" last May -- will lure boxing fans into laying out $19.95 to see "Lady Willpower", Anissa "The Annhilator" and their sisters ply their trades.

Kulis won't reveal the number of pay-per-view "buys" for "Lips of Rouge" because he says it was a small test promotion. But this time Kulis is heavily promoting "Leather and Lace" and says he already has another boxing show from the distaff side set for October 18.

Fans' acceptance of women coming out of the boxing closet recently can be traced to the national exposure of Christy Martin in the last couple of years, aided mightily by Mike Tyson's dismal first few fights when he resumed his career shortly after leaving prison in 1995.

As Tyson quickly dispatched a collection of barely-warm bodies until he ran into Evander Holyfield twice, the most entertaining fighter by far on the cards was Martin, a free-swinging slugger from West Virginia, dubbed "The Coal Miner's Daughter."

Of course Martin helped herself with her sharp eye for self-promotion with her trademark pink blur of punches concocted from pink shoes, shorts and top, finished off with lots of makeup, including her favourite "Hot Cinnamon" lipstick and "Warm Ginger" blush.

But Martin would still be fighting in beer-soaked tents at county fairs for hamburger money if it were not for promoter Don King, who put his high-octane promotional skills behind her. And now, after an acrimonious dispute over her pay, King and Martin, who appears exclusively on King's cards, have settled on about $100,000 per fight for the former school teacher.
The "Leather and Lace" women are fighting for better than "chump" change, as the saying goes, but they are nowhere near Martin-like paydays.
Bonnie "The Cobra," "Battling" Beverly, Nora "The Canadian Cannon" and their colleagues will make a minimum of $200 for each round they are scheduled to fight, Kulis said.

Kulis would not divulge the highest pay for the night's work because he has negotiated separately with each fighter and likely wants to avoid explaining to angry, tough women wearing boxing gloves the differences in his perception of their worth. He did say, however, some of the women would earn $4,000.
Kulis and others claim that pound for pound, women are often more entertaining than the men who are having more than a little trouble with their credibility these days.
That's due in part to "Mighty" Mike Tyson, who against Holyfield turned into "Masticating" Mikey, a petulant two-year-old who needs to be taught not to bite when things don't go his way.

And there is Andrew Golata, who gave new meaning to "fear of success" when -- ahead on scorecards and pumelling Riddick Bowe -- he snatched defeat from victory by delivering a series of low blows to let Bowe win twice by default. Roy Jones, Jr. became another example of blatant thuggery in the ring recently when he clubbed an opponent senseless while he was down.
So bring on the women, promoters and cable television types say.
"When they come out and are all offence, all blood, and they pound each other -- that's what the fans want," Kulis said.
That may be but that's not Yvonne Trevino's preferred image of herself.
Trevino, from Peoria, Arizona, acknowledges that fans are "hungry for the blood."
But the 30-year-old mother of a young girl says she wants "to impress with skill and technique" when she fights for the International Female Boxing Association bantamweight title on Saturday.
Trevino says she dropped her old kickboxing monicker "The Terminator" because she wants to distance herself from what she said is the "sideshow" aspect of women's boxing.
But it's difficult to imagine promoters ever wanting to change the sideshow titilation factor that seems inherent in selling women's boxing.
It seems a stretch to ever imagine promoters pushing Mirriam "The Mom", Harriet "The Homemaker", or Barbara "The Baker".
